chapters.title: How to make a noise
chapters.intro: By the end of this chapter, you will have built a machine that translates electricity into sound.
chapters.payoff:
You may have noticed a pattern:
- A pitch is voltage (`2V` for middle C, `+/- 1V` per octave)
- A control signal (`cv`) is voltage
- The audio signal sent to the `Output` module is voltage

So you may be wondering, *What if I mix and match? What happens if I use an oscillator signal as a control voltage? What about as a pitch signal?*

If so, you're exactly the kind of pervert who is going to really enjoy analog synthesis.
chapters.challenge:
Find out what happens![^1]


[^1]: Hint: add another oscillator module and use it in a dastardly manner.

steps.title: Enable audio
steps.text: Click `Enable audio` in the sidebar.

steps.title: The patch
steps.text:
A *patch* is a catch-all term for any configuration of interconnected synth modules. The term comes from the *patch cables* we use to connect analog synth modules.[^1]

# Click `NEW PATCH` in the sidebar. 

[^1]: Long ago, patch cables were used to hot-swap spare equipment into vital communications systems in which something had melted, burned out, or exploded. 

    These days, patch cables are mostly used by recreational drug users, commodity fetishists, and the neurodivergent in order to make things go *wubwubwubwub*

steps.title: Add an Oscillator
steps.text:
`Main` here is what is going to send the information from our keyboard circulating through our patch. 

Its two most important functions are to send `pitch` (i.e., what note is being played) and `gate`, which answers yes or no to the question, "Is a key being held down right now?"[^1]

The output of `Output` is what you hear. It's can be thought of as the rectum of a patch. A synth patch poops sound into the toilet of the ear.

# Add an `Oscillator` module using the sidebar button or command palette (`Ctrl/Cmd+K` or the `/` key). 

Any module on the canvas can be moved around by clicking on its header and dragging it around.

[^1]: The caveats, exceptions, and backpedaling that go here are on our feature roadmap and are slated to be added in Q3 of FY 2029

steps.title: Oscillators
steps.text:
An *oscillator* is a machine named after what it does. It oscillates.[^1] 

Want it to stop oscillating? Too bad. If it stopped, that would constitute behavior that synth experts call `not oscillating`. For that you would need a completely different kind of machine.[^2]

## Connect `main`’s pitch output to the `Oscillator’s` pitch input with a patch cable (click one jack and drag to the other jack). 

Congratulations! Your machine makes noise.  This noise is continuous.

[^1]: Oscillation is any continuous fluctuation over time that is centered around some central value. Synth oscillators emit continuously fluctuating voltage -- traditionally anywhere from 5V to -5V, centered around 0V. 

[^2]: These machines are pricey, because they have only ever been made by one company. That company is called Teenage Engineering

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator
steps.text:
Press some keys on the home row of your computer keyboard. You should hear your noise change pitch. 

You can do this for a while, but eventually your ears and brain will start to hurt. 

When you've had enough, **click on the patch cable between `Oscillator`'s `out` jack and `Output`'s `in` jack to remove the cable.**

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator (cont'd)
steps.text:
Obviously, it would be impractical to unplug your oscillator every time you want a note to stop sounding. Luckily, there is a solution: the *voltage-controlled amplifier (VCA)*.

## Add a VCA module. 

A VCA has two important inputs: `in`, for an audio signal, and `cv`, for control voltage. Its `output` is just those two signals multiplied together. 

In the next step, we're going to use a VCA to multiply `Oscillator`'s  output voltage by zero. This is how we shut up an oscillator.

steps.title: Shutting up an oscillator (cont'd) (cont'd)
steps.text:
Let's put the VCA to work.

## 1. Drag the Oscillator’s out jack to the VCA’s in jack. 

## 2. Drag the VCA’s out jack to Output’s l jack.

Silence. The Oscillator is still oscillating, but the VCA is closed: nothing is plugged into its `control voltage` jack.

## 3.  Drag `main`'s `gate` jack to VCA's `cv` jack.

## 4. Press a key on your keyboard's home row. Play a little ditty.

This little machine is starting to resemble an instrument.

steps.title: Gates
steps.text:
Whenever you press a key, here's what's happening:

- The sustained electrical voltage coming through `Main`'s  `pitch` jack changes to represent the pressed key's pitch. `2V` means middle C (aka `C4`). Each volt up or down from there represents an octave. [^1]
- `Main`'s `gate` output voltage, which rests at `0V`, suddenly spikes to `5V`.
- The output signal of `VCA`, which is using `Main`'s gate signal as its *control voltage* signal multiplier, suddenly spikes from `0V` to the oscillator's signal voltage multiplied by 5.

[^1]: So the note one octave up from `C4` (aka `C5`) is represented as `3V`.  One semitone up from that (aka `C#5`) is represented as `3.083V`. Why `.083`? Because there are 12 notes in an octave, and `1V/12 = 0.083̅V`.

steps.title: Seeing sound
steps.text:
To the left of the Oscillator’s `out` jack you'll find a little grey ◎ button.

## Click it.

The window that just popped up is what's called an *oscilloscope*. 

What you see there is a live visualization of the oscillator's output voltage over time.  You may recognize this squiggle from high school math class as a *wave*.  

Conveniently, sound can also be represented as a wave.

*Analog audio* gets its name from the strategy of using changes in voltage as an *analogy* for changes in air pressure.

parts.label: Click ◎ beside the Oscillator’s out

steps.title: Change the wave
steps.text:
The shape of a wave determines its timbre. 

Right now, our oscillator emits a `sine` wave -- reminscent of a french horn.  But there are a few other types of wave it can emit  -- hold a note and move its `wave` slider around to hear what they sound like.

parts.label: Listen with Note or Riff, or play your keyboard

chapters.title: Shaping a note
chapters.intro: A gate is on or off, so the note it opens is on or off too. Real notes have a shape: they start, hold and die away. The envelope generator (ADSR: attack, decay, sustain, release) draws that shape each time the gate opens, and the VCA follows it instead of the bare gate.
chapters.payoff: One oscillator now speaks with two different shapes: a swelling pad and a pluck.
chapters.challenge: Make a tiny bell or a very slow sunrise; save both variations.

steps.title: Add an ADSR
steps.text: Add an ADSR. Its env output rises when the gate opens, falls to the sustain level, and dies away after the gate closes.

steps.title: Let the envelope drive the gain
steps.text: Cable Main gate → ADSR gate and ADSR env → VCA cv, then click the cable from Main’s gate to the VCA to remove it. The note now has a shape.

steps.title: Draw the shape
steps.text: Drag the ADSR’s a (attack) to about 0.3 s and r (release) to about 1 s. Hold a note: it swells in and fades out after you let go.
steps.why: Attack and release are times, sustain is a level. Pads have long attacks and releases; the next step makes the opposite.

parts.label: Set a (attack) to 0.1 s or more
Set r (release) to 0.5 s or more

steps.title: Make it percussive
steps.text: Set a (attack) to 0.005 s, s (sustain) to 0 and d (decay) to about 0.2 s. Hold a note: it rings out and dies although the key is still down. Plucked and struck sounds have no sustain.

parts.label: Set a (attack) to 0.01 s or less
Set s (sustain) to 0
Set d (decay) to 0.4 s or less

steps.title: A pluck or a pad?
steps.text: Start Riff and hear the pluck die before the next note. Optional: compare attack 0.3 s, sustain 0.6, release 1 s for a swelling pad; then restore attack 0.005 s and sustain 0 to continue the pluck lesson. The contrast is time and shape, not a new oscillator.

steps.title: A slider thumb is a jack
steps.text: Set the wave to square (pulse width only matters for a square). Then Alt-drag the thumb of the Oscillator’s pw slider onto the ADSR’s env jack (or drag from env and drop it on the thumb). The envelope now also sweeps the pulse width.
steps.why: Dropping a signal on a thumb routes it through one of the module’s parameter inputs, p1 or p2. The same envelope shapes two things at once: loudness and timbre.

parts.label: Set the Oscillator’s wave to square
Drop the ADSR’s env on the pw thumb (Alt-drag the thumb to env)

steps.title: Undo and redo
steps.text: Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac), or Commands → Undo: the route is gone. Press Shift+Ctrl+Z (Commands → Redo) and it is back. Forty steps of history are kept, cables and modules included.

parts.label: Bring the env → pw route back (redo)

chapters.title: Subtractive voice
chapters.intro: Subtractive synthesis starts with a bright wave and takes harmonics away with a filter. The cutoff says where the filter starts cutting, the resonance adds a peak there. Moving the cutoff with an envelope, an LFO or a knob is where most of the classic synth sounds come from.
chapters.payoff: Your filter can move by itself and follow a performance knob.
chapters.challenge: Find the moment where a gentle wah becomes a rhythm.

steps.title: Add a Filter
steps.text: Add a Filter and put it between the Oscillator and the VCA: Oscillator out → Filter in, Filter lp24 → VCA in, and remove the cable from the Oscillator to the VCA.
steps.why: VCO → VCF → VCA is the classic subtractive chain. lp24 is a 24 dB low pass: steep. lp12 is gentler, hp lets the highs through instead.

steps.title: Sweep the cutoff
steps.text: Start Riff and drag cutoff down from 16 kHz to about 400 Hz: the tone gets darker. Move slowly and hear the upper harmonics disappear. Leave cutoff below 800 Hz.
steps.why: The cutoff slider is logarithmic, like pitch: every octave gets the same distance. Resonance feeds a little of the output back, which makes the filter ring at its cutoff.

parts.label: Set cutoff to 800 Hz or below

steps.title: Give the cutoff a voice
steps.text: Keep Riff playing and raise Filter res to about 0.6. A whistle appears at the cutoff. Optional: sweep cutoff to hear the peak travel, then return it below 800 Hz before continuing.

parts.label: Set res to 0.5 or more

steps.title: Track the keyboard
steps.text: Tick track. The cutoff now follows the note, one octave per octave, so high notes stay as bright as low ones. Play up and down.

parts.label: Tick track

steps.title: Add an LFO
steps.text: Add an LFO (low frequency oscillator). It is an oscillator too slow to hear, made to move other things. Set its rate to about 0.5 Hz.

parts.label: Add an LFO
Set its rate to 1 Hz or below

steps.title: Wobble the cutoff
steps.text: Drag the LFO’s out to the Filter’s cv jack. The grey route shows cv is built into cutoff; cvamt sets how far it reaches: set it to 2 oct. Hold a note.
steps.why: The cv input is additive in octaves: a signal of 1 moves the cutoff up by cvamt octaves. Pins p1 and p2 work differently: they reach any parameter you tick in its ⋯ menu.

parts.label: Set cvamt to 1.5 oct or more

steps.title: From a slow wah to a wobble
steps.text: Start Riff. Optional: try LFO rate 0.5 Hz, then 4 Hz. The same cutoff movement becomes a rhythm. Return to 0.5 Hz before continuing; keep notes short if the high resonance is sharp.

steps.title: One knob, two parameters
steps.text: Drag Main’s blue k1 jack to the Filter’s p1. Open the ⋯ menu of cutoff and tick P1; do the same for res. Main’s k1 slider stands for the first knob of the FM-1.
steps.why: The matrix in the ⋯ menu decides which parameters a pin reaches. A blue tick appears on each slider the knob reaches: that is where the knob alone holds the parameter.

steps.title: Set the depth
steps.text: In the ⋯ menu of cutoff, drag the p1 attenuverter to about 0.5: the knob now reaches half as far. A negative value turns the knob around.

parts.label: Move the p1 attenuverter off 1 (⋯ menu of cutoff)

steps.title: Live value and base value
steps.text: Hold a note and watch the cutoff slider: the thumb follows the live, wobbling value and a tick marks the base. Now move Main’s k1 slider: the blue ticks move, and so does the sound.

chapters.title: Your first assembly
chapters.intro: An assembly packs modules into one card that shows only the ports and knobs you choose. It can be saved to your library, reused in other patches, and put inside other assemblies. The five modules you built are about to become one instrument.
chapters.payoff: Five modules fold into your first reusable instrument.
chapters.challenge: Give the instrument a stage name and keep a personal variation.

steps.title: Select the modules
steps.text: Shift-click the Oscillator, Filter, ADSR, VCA and LFO, or drag a box around them on the empty canvas. Selected cards get a highlight. Main and Output stay outside.

parts.label: Select the Oscillator, Filter, ADSR, VCA and LFO

steps.title: Group them
steps.text: Press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G on a Mac), or Commands → Make assembly, and name it My voice. The five cards fold into one that shows the ports which had cables from outside: pitch, gate and out.
steps.why: Grouping changes nothing in the sound. Ports with outside cables are exposed automatically; the rest is hidden until you expose it.

parts.label: Group the Oscillator, Filter, ADSR, VCA and LFO (Ctrl+G)

steps.title: Open it up
steps.text: Click expand on the My voice card. A frame shows the modules inside; every port and slider has a ○ toggle.

parts.label: Expand the assembly

steps.title: Put two knobs on the card
steps.text: Click ○ next to the Filter’s cutoff and next to the ADSR’s r. They become sliders on the collapsed card. Click ○ beside the LFO’s out too: an extra output.

steps.title: Resize the frame
steps.text: Drag the ◢ corner of the frame to give the cards room (the arrow keys work on it too). Cards can be moved inside the frame; dragging one out takes it out of the assembly.

steps.title: Close it
steps.text: Click collapse in the frame’s header. One card: pitch, gate, out, the LFO’s out, cutoff and r. Play it.

parts.label: Collapse the assembly

steps.title: Five modules, one instrument
steps.text: Play your new instrument. Move the exposed cutoff and release sliders: one changes color, the other changes the tail. Optional: give the card a personal name, then use My voice for the library save so later chapters can find it.

steps.title: Save it to your library
steps.text: Click save on the card and keep the name My voice. It is now in the Library tab and in + Add assembly, under Your library, ready for any patch.

steps.title: Fit the patch to the screen
steps.text: Commands → Fit patch to screen scales the canvas so everything is in view. Ctrl+wheel (pinch on touch) zooms freely; Reset canvas scale goes back to 100 %.

chapters.title: An effect assembly
chapters.intro: An effect is a module with audio in and audio out. Delay repeats, reverb smears the repeats into a room, chorus thickens with detuned copies. Each has a mix slider: dry signal against wet. Chained, they become one effect you can save and reuse.
chapters.payoff: Your instrument carries a room, echoes and stereo movement.
chapters.challenge: Make a small room and an impossible cavern. Compare each with bypass.

steps.title: Hear one echo
steps.text: Add Delay. Cable My voice out → Delay in and Delay out → Output l. Remove My voice out → Output l. Tap Note, then Release notes: the repeats continue after the note. Try mix at 0, then 0.4.

parts.label: Cable My voice out → Delay in
Remove the old cable My voice out → Output l (click it)

steps.title: Put the echoes in a room
steps.text: Add Reverb. Cable Delay out → Reverb in and Reverb out → Output l; remove Delay out → Output l. Compare size 0.2 and 0.8: a small room versus a long wash. These are optional listening settings.

steps.title: Spread the sound
steps.text: Add Chorus. Cable Reverb out → Chorus in, Chorus l → Output l and Chorus r → Output r; remove Reverb out → Output l. Start Riff and compare Chorus mix 0 and 0.5: the sound widens. Leave the mix you like.

steps.title: Tune the space
steps.text: Set the Delay’s time to about 375 ms and fb (feedback) to 0.5, and the Reverb’s size to 0.7. Play a short note and listen to the tail.
steps.why: Feedback sends the delayed signal back into the line: each repeat is quieter than the last. Above 0.9 the repeats barely fade.

parts.label: Set the Delay’s time to 300 ms or more
Set the Delay’s fb to 0.4 or more
Set the Reverb’s size to 0.6 or more

steps.title: Hear it with and without
steps.text: Click the Reverb card to select it and press B (or click ⏻ in its header): the module is bypassed and passes its input straight through. Press B again to switch it back on.

parts.label: Press B twice on the Reverb (off, then on)
Switch the Reverb back on

steps.title: Group the three
steps.text: Select the Delay, Reverb and Chorus and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G). Name the assembly My space. Its card shows in, l and r.

parts.label: Group the Delay, Reverb and Chorus (Ctrl+G)

steps.title: Choose its knobs
steps.text: Expand My space, click ○ on the Delay’s time and mix and on the Reverb’s mix, then collapse it. An effect needs few knobs on the outside.

steps.title: Save My space
steps.text: Click save on the My space card. Your library now holds an instrument and an effect; the next chapters use both.

chapters.title: Second instrument: FM
chapters.intro: In frequency modulation one oscillator, the modulator, wobbles the phase of another, the carrier, thousands of times a second. The wobble creates new harmonics: the ratio of the two pitches sets which ones, the depth sets how many. An envelope on the depth makes the classic bright-then-mellow electric piano.
chapters.payoff: Two pure tones became a playable FM instrument with its own space.
chapters.challenge: Save a mellow key and a metallic bell from the same two oscillators.

steps.title: An oscillator, cabled to the pitch
steps.text: Add an Oscillator and cable Main pitch → Oscillator pitch. Leave the wave on sine: FM wants pure tones.

steps.title: Hear the carrier first
steps.text: Add a VCA. Cable the Oscillator out → VCA in, Main gate → VCA cv, and VCA out → Output l. Play Note: a pure sine. Stop it before adding the second oscillator.

steps.title: Duplicate it
steps.text: Click the Oscillator to select it and press Ctrl+D (Cmd+D), or Commands → Duplicate selection. The copy keeps its settings. Cables from outside the selection are not copied: connect Main pitch to the new Oscillator’s pitch.

parts.label: Duplicate the Oscillator (Ctrl+D)
Cable Main pitch → the second Oscillator’s pitch

steps.title: Modulator into carrier
steps.text: Cable the second Oscillator’s out into the first one’s pm input, and set the first one’s pm slider (the depth) to about 2. The first is now the carrier, the second the modulator.
steps.why: pm is phase modulation, what the DX7 and this engine do; it sounds like FM. The depth slider is the modulation index: 0 is a sine, 8 is a wall of harmonics.

parts.label: Set the carrier’s pm slider to 1 or more

steps.title: Set the ratio
steps.text: Set the modulator’s coarse to +12: an octave above the carrier, a 2:1 ratio, hollow like a clarinet. Try +19 (3:1) and +7 for a bell-like clang.
steps.why: Whole-number ratios give harmonic spectra; odd ratios like 1.41 give inharmonic, metallic ones. coarse is in semitones.

parts.label: Move the modulator’s coarse off 0

steps.title: Three colors from two sines
steps.text: Start Riff. Optional: compare modulator coarse +12 with pm 1 (hollow), coarse +7 with pm 4 (metallic), then coarse +12 with pm 0.3 (mellow). Return pm to 2 and coarse to +12 before continuing. Save your favorite as a named variation.

steps.title: Loudness from a level / rate envelope
steps.text: Add an Env L/R. Remove Main gate → VCA cv. Cable carrier out → VCA in, Main gate → Env gate, Env env → VCA cv, VCA out → Output l.
steps.why: Env L/R is the DX7 envelope: four levels and the rate to reach each one. The last level, l4, is where the note ends after the key is released.

parts.label: Cable Main gate → Env gate
Cable Env env → VCA cv

steps.title: Brightness from the same envelope
steps.text: Alt-drag the carrier’s pm thumb onto the Env’s env jack. Set the Env’s l2 and l3 to 0.3 and r2 to 0.4 s: the note starts bright and mellows while it decays.

parts.label: Drop the Env’s env on the carrier’s pm thumb
Set the Env’s l2 to 0.3
Set the Env’s l3 to 0.3
Set the Env’s r2 to about 0.4 s

steps.title: Group it as FM keys
steps.text: Select both Oscillators, the Env and the VCA and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G). Name it FM keys. It exposes pitch (twice, one per oscillator), gate and out.

parts.label: Group both Oscillators, the Env and the VCA (Ctrl+G)

steps.title: Insert My space
steps.text: Click + Add assembly and pick My space under Your library (the one you saved in chapter 5). It arrives as one card.

parts.label: Insert My space from your library

steps.title: Put the effect behind the keys
steps.text: Cable FM keys out → My space in, My space l → Output l and My space r → Output r. Remove the cable from FM keys to Output.

parts.label: Cable FM keys out → My space in
Cable My space l → Output l
Cable My space r → Output r
Remove the old cable FM keys out → Output l (click it)

steps.title: Nest the effect inside the instrument
steps.text: Expand FM keys and drag the My space card into its frame by its header: it becomes part of FM keys, which now exposes l and r itself. Collapse FM keys.
steps.why: Assemblies nest three levels deep. An instrument that carries its own effect is one card wherever you use it.

steps.title: Save FM keys
steps.text: Click save on the FM keys card. My space travels inside it.

chapters.title: Plucked and struck
chapters.intro: Physical models start from how real instruments work: a burst of energy goes into something that resonates. String is a Karplus-Strong string, a short delay line fed back on itself. Modal is a set of tuned resonances like a bar or a bell. Comb is a resonator you can excite with anything, even noise.
chapters.payoff: You built a string, a resonating body and a breathy pipe.
chapters.challenge: Write a three-note call and answer with muted and ringing settings.

steps.title: A string
steps.text: Add a String. Cable Main pitch → String pitch, Main gate → String gate and String out → Output l. Each key plucks it.

steps.title: Let it ring
steps.text: Set the String’s decay to about 4 s and damp to 0.1: a long, bright note. Optional: switch burst to pulse for a harder pick.
steps.why: The string is a delay line as long as one period, with feedback. decay sets how much is fed back, damp how fast the highs are lost on each round trip.

parts.label: Set decay to 3 s or more
Set damp to 0.15 or less

steps.title: Play chords
steps.text: On the Main card set voices to 4. The String card shows ×4: it runs once per voice. Hold a chord.
steps.why: Every module that hears pitch, gate or velocity runs once per voice; effects and the Output stay single and sum the voices.

steps.title: Strike a body with it
steps.text: Add a Modal. Cable String out → Modal in and Modal out → Output r. Set struct to 0.5 and decay to 2 s: the string now rings a bell-like body.

parts.label: Set struct to 0.3 or more
Set Modal decay to about 2 s

steps.title: Muted string, ringing body
steps.text: Use Chord with four voices. Optional: try String damp 0.8 for a muted pick, then 0.1 for a ringing string. Bypass Modal to hear the dry string on the left; turn it back on to hear the body on the right. Return damp to 0.1 before continuing.

steps.title: Blow noise through a comb
steps.text: Add Noise, a Comb and a VCA. Cable Noise out → Comb in, Main pitch → Comb pitch, Comb out → VCA in, Main gate → VCA cv, VCA out → Output l.
steps.why: A comb filter is a tuned delay line: noise through it rings at the note, like breath through a pipe. The VCA is a simple on / off here, straight from the gate.

parts.label: Add Noise

steps.title: Make it ring
steps.text: Set the Comb’s fb to 0.95 and damp to 0.1: the noise turns into a breathy, whistling tone at the note.

parts.label: Set the Comb’s fb to 0.9 or more
Set Comb damp to 0.1

steps.title: Separate the breath from the string
steps.text: Optional: bypass String and Modal, then play Note to hear only noise through Comb. Change Comb damp from 0.1 to 0.8: the breath loses its whistle. Switch both models back on and return damp to 0.1 when finished.

steps.title: Slide between notes
steps.text: Add a Glide. Cable Main pitch → Glide in and Glide out → Comb pitch, and remove the cable from Main’s pitch to the Comb. Set time to 0.3 s and play two notes.
steps.why: Glide (portamento) slews a control signal: the pitch takes time to arrive. It works on any control cable, not only pitch.

parts.label: Set Glide time to about 0.3 s

steps.title: Group the pluck
steps.text: Select the String and the Modal and press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G). Name it Pluck. Expand it, click ○ on the String’s decay and the Modal’s struct, and collapse it again.

parts.label: Group the String and the Modal (Ctrl+G)
Collapse the assembly

steps.title: Save Pluck
steps.text: Click save on the Pluck card. Chapter 10 plays it from a melody machine.

chapters.title: Wavetables and grains
chapters.intro: A wavetable oscillator holds a row of waveforms and sweeps through them: the timbre moves without a filter. A granular module chops audio into grains a few milliseconds long and scatters them in time and pitch: a cloud out of a note. This patch starts with four voices so Chord can fill the granular buffer. Both are texture tools; zoom out as the canvas grows.
chapters.payoff: You can turn a vowel into a moving, frozen cloud.
chapters.challenge: Capture a chord and find a texture that sounds nothing like its source.

steps.title: A wavetable oscillator
steps.text: Add a Wavetable and cable Main pitch → Wavetable pitch. Set bank to formant. Next we give it a gated output, then listen to the vowels.

parts.label: Set bank to formant

steps.title: Hear a vowel
steps.text: Add a VCA. Cable Wavetable out → VCA in, Main gate → VCA cv and VCA out → Output l. Start Note and move Wavetable pos: the vowel changes. The VCA keeps the sound under your control.

steps.title: Sweep the table
steps.text: Add an LFO with rate 0.2 Hz. Alt-drag the Wavetable’s pos thumb onto the LFO’s out (or drop the LFO’s cable on the thumb). The position now sweeps on its own.

parts.label: Add an LFO
Drop the LFO’s out on the pos thumb
Set the LFO’s rate to 0.5 Hz or below

steps.title: A slow envelope
steps.text: Add an ADSR. Remove Main gate → VCA cv. Cable Main gate → ADSR gate, ADSR env → VCA cv, Wavetable out → VCA in. Set a to 1 s and r to 2 s: a pad.

parts.label: Set a to 0.5 s or more
Set r to 1 s or more

steps.title: Into the cloud
steps.text: Add a Granular. Cable VCA out → Granular in and Main gate → Granular trig. Cable Granular out → Output l and remove VCA out → Output l. Set size to 0.15 s, density to 40, spray to 0.5 and pitch to +12.
steps.why: The granular module records what comes in and plays tiny windows of it, spread over position, time and pitch. spray is how far the grains wander from the position.

parts.label: Set size to about 0.15 s
Set density to 40
Set spray to 0.3 or more
Move pitch off 0

steps.title: Keep a moment in a cloud
steps.text: With Main voices at 4, play Chord for two seconds to fill the buffer, then switch Granular freeze on. Stop the notes: the captured sound remains. Optional: change pitch and spray, then turn freeze off before continuing. Bypass Granular to compare the dry pad.

steps.title: Place it in the stereo field
steps.text: Add a Pan. Cable Granular out → Pan in, Pan l → Output l, Pan r → Output r. Remove Granular out → Output l. Then drop the LFO’s out on the pan slider’s thumb: pos is the Pan’s built-in input, so the cable goes there.

parts.label: Cable LFO out → Pan pos (drop it on the pan thumb)

steps.title: A phaser on the way out
steps.text: Add a Phaser between the Granular and the Pan: Granular out → Phaser in, Phaser out → Pan in, and remove the cable from the Granular to the Pan.

steps.title: Zoom out
steps.text: Nine cards no longer fit. Hold Ctrl (Cmd) and scroll to zoom, pinch on a touch screen, or use Commands → Fit patch to screen.

steps.title: Watch the cloud
steps.text: Click ◎ on the Granular’s out and switch the scope to Spectrum. Hold a note: the grains smear the harmonics into a band.

parts.label: Click ◎ beside the Granular’s out

chapters.title: Two instruments, one keyboard
chapters.intro: Layering is two instruments on one keyboard. A mixer sums them, the arpeggiator plays held keys as a pattern, a macro range gives a knob a useful stretch, and the morph slider fades between two settings of the whole patch.
chapters.payoff: Your two instruments play together, and a single slider moves their balance.
chapters.challenge: Find a halfway morph you prefer to either endpoint.

steps.title: Insert My voice
steps.text: Click + Add assembly and pick My voice from Your library. Cable Main pitch → its pitch and Main gate → its gate.

parts.label: Insert My voice from your library
Cable Main pitch → My voice pitch
Cable Main gate → My voice gate

steps.title: Insert FM keys
steps.text: Insert FM keys the same way. Its card shows two pitch inputs, one per oscillator, and a gate.

parts.label: Insert FM keys from your library

steps.title: Merge the two pitch inputs
steps.text: Expand FM keys. Next to one of the exposed pitch inputs open merge into… and choose the other pitch. One pitch jack now feeds both oscillators. Collapse it.
steps.why: A merged input sends one cable to several inner inputs. Split undoes it.

parts.label: Merge the two pitch inputs of FM keys (merge into…)

steps.title: Cable the second instrument
steps.text: Cable Main pitch → FM keys pitch and Main gate → FM keys gate. Both instruments are ready for the mixer in the next step.

parts.label: Cable Main pitch → FM keys pitch
Cable Main gate → FM keys gate

steps.title: Mix them
steps.text: Add a Mixer 4. Cable My voice out → in1, FM keys l → in2, FM keys r → in3, and Mixer out → Output l and r. l1..l4 are the levels.

parts.label: Cable My voice out → Mixer in1
Cable FM keys l → Mixer in2
Cable FM keys r → Mixer in3
Cable Mixer out → Output l
Cable Mixer out → Output r

steps.title: Hear what each layer contributes
steps.text: Start Riff. Optional: put Mixer l2 and l3 at 0 to hear My voice alone; restore them, then put l1 at 0 to hear FM keys alone. Bring l1 back up until neither layer hides the other. This balance is your choice.

steps.title: Let the arpeggiator play
steps.text: Open the arp panel on the Main card and press Space (or Commands → arpeggiator). Hold a chord: the keys are played one after another at the rate shown.

parts.label: Enable the arpeggiator (Space)

steps.title: A knob with a range
steps.text: Cable Main k2 → My voice p1 (the pin of the Filter inside). Open the ⋯ menu of My voice’s cutoff, tick P1 and Map between two values, then set the ends to 150 Hz and 4000 Hz. Set the Filter’s P1 depth to 1 so the knob reaches both ends.
steps.why: A macro range maps the knob’s whole travel onto a slice of the parameter: the useful part of the cutoff instead of 20 Hz to 16 kHz.

parts.label: Cable Main k2 → My voice p1

steps.title: Compare two snapshots
steps.text: Commands → Set snapshot A. Change a few sliders (cutoff, the mixer levels), then Commands → Set snapshot B. Press Alt+B to flip between them. Listen to the change in balance: snapshots switch the whole patch instantly. The next step makes a continuous fade.

steps.title: Fade between the snapshots
steps.text: On Main, open the B side picker and choose Snapshot B. Move morph from 0 to 1, then leave it halfway. You now hear a continuous change in the mixer balance; Alt+B alone only switches snapshots.
steps.why: A morph target must have the same modules and cables. Snapshot B is a complete compatible patch; selecting it copies its parameters into the B side. Main itself is not morphed.

parts.label: Set Main morph between 0 and 1

chapters.title: A random melody machine
chapters.intro: A sequencer is a clock and a value per step. A random one samples noise on every tick; a quantizer snaps the values to a scale so they become notes; a pulse turns each tick into a gate of a chosen length. The instruments you saved will play whatever the machine comes up with.
chapters.payoff: Chance and a written sequence now share one musical clock.
chapters.challenge: Write a four-note answer to the random machine.

steps.title: A clock
steps.text: Add an LFO, set its wave to square and its rate to 4 Hz. A square wave is a clock: its rising edge is a tick.

parts.label: Add an LFO
Set its wave to square
Set its rate to 2 Hz or more

steps.title: Divide it
steps.text: Add a Clock div and cable LFO out → Clock div clock. Its outputs out, d2, d4 and d8 tick every div, 2, 4 and 8 ticks.

steps.title: A random value per tick
steps.text: Add Noise and an S&H (sample and hold). Cable Noise out → S&H in and Clock div out → S&H clock. On every tick the S&H grabs the noise’s value and holds it.

parts.label: Add Noise
Add an S&H

steps.title: Snap it to a scale
steps.text: Add a Quantizer, cable S&H out → Quantizer in and set scale to pent min. Random voltages become notes of a pentatonic minor scale.
steps.why: Pitch is a control signal: one unit per octave, a semitone is a twelfth. The quantizer rounds to the nearest note of the scale, which is why random noise sounds like a melody.

parts.label: Set scale to pent min

steps.title: Play Pluck with it
steps.text: Insert Pluck from Your library. Cable Quantizer out → Pluck pitch, Clock div out → Pluck gate and Pluck out → Output l. The machine plays on its own now.

parts.label: Insert Pluck from your library

steps.title: FM keys on every second tick
steps.text: Add a Pulse with time 0.05 s and cable Clock div d2 → Pulse trig. Insert FM keys; cable Quantizer out → FM keys pitch, Pulse out → FM keys gate, FM keys l → Output r.
steps.why: A divider passes selected input pulses with their original width. Pulse makes a predictable 0.05 s gate regardless of the clock’s pulse width.

parts.label: Set the Pulse’s time to 0.1 s or less
Insert FM keys from your library
Cable Quantizer out → FM keys pitch
Cable Pulse out → FM keys gate
Cable FM keys l → Output r

steps.title: Let chance write the first phrase
steps.text: Listen for several repeats before replacing the random source. Optional: change Quantizer scale and hear the same random movement obey another set of notes. Return to pent min; the next step lets you write a four-note reply.

steps.title: A written melody instead
steps.text: Add a Sequencer, cable Clock div out → Sequencer clock and Sequencer out → Quantizer in, and remove the cable from the S&H to the Quantizer. Set s1..s4 to a few different values; len to 4.
steps.why: The Sequencer’s steps are the same kind of signal the S&H made, just chosen by you. Through the quantizer the steps land on scale notes whatever you set them to.

parts.label: Set len to 4 or less

steps.title: Lock to the arpeggiator’s clock
steps.text: Cable Main clock → Clock div clock and remove the LFO’s cable to it; set the Clock div’s div to 6. Add a second Clock div: first out → second clock, second d2 → Pulse trig; remove first d2 → Pulse trig. Press Space: Main’s clock now ticks 24 times per beat at the arp tempo, and on the FM-1 it follows MIDI clock.

parts.label: Set the first Clock div’s div to 6
Cable first divider out → second divider clock
Cable second divider d2 → Pulse trig
Remove the old cable first divider d2 → Pulse trig (click it)

steps.title: Hear the machine lock together
steps.text: Press Space to start the arpeggiator clock. Change Main’s tempo: the written melody, Pluck and every-second-tick FM part stay together. Optional: change s1–s4 to write a four-note answer to the random melody.

parts.label: Start the arpeggiator clock (Space)

chapters.title: Drums from noise
chapters.intro: Most drum sounds are noise or a short tone with a very fast envelope. A hi-hat is filtered noise that dies in a tenth of a second; a kick is a sine whose pitch drops; a snare is both. You build the hat, borrow the kick and snare from the library, and clock them from a divider.
chapters.payoff: Noise became a hat, a kit, and a small performance with your own instruments.
chapters.challenge: Perform eight bars: establish the beat, bring in the melody, add a fill, return home.

steps.title: Noise through a high pass
steps.text: Add Noise and a Filter. Cable Noise out → Filter in and set the cutoff to about 6 kHz: the Filter’s hp output is the hiss of a hat.

parts.label: Add Noise
Set cutoff to 4 kHz or more

steps.title: A very short envelope
steps.text: Add an Env L/R and a VCA. Cable Filter hp → VCA in, Main gate → Env gate, Env env → VCA cv, VCA out → Output l. Set l1 to 1, r1 to 0.001 s, l2 to 0, r2 to 0.08 s, l3 to 0 and l4 to 0. Hold a key: one crisp hiss dies away and stays silent.

parts.label: Cable Main gate → Env gate
Cable Env env → VCA cv
Set l1 to 1
Set r1 to 0.001 s
Set l2 to 0
Set r2 to about 0.08 s
Set l3 to 0
Set l4 to 0

steps.title: Group it as Hat and save it
steps.text: Select the Noise, Filter, Env and VCA, press Ctrl+G (Cmd+G) and name it Hat. Click save on its card.

parts.label: Group the Noise, Filter, Env and VCA (Ctrl+G)

steps.title: Borrow a kick and a snare
steps.text: Click + Add assembly and insert kick and snare from the Drums shelf. Expand one to see how it is built: a kick is a sine with a pitch envelope.

parts.label: Insert the factory kick (Drums shelf)
Insert the factory snare (Drums shelf)

steps.title: A clock and a divider
steps.text: Add an LFO (square, 8 Hz) and a Clock div with div 2. Cable LFO out → Clock div clock.

parts.label: Add an LFO
Set the LFO’s wave to square
Set the LFO’s rate to 6 Hz or more
Set the Clock div’s div to 2

steps.title: A pattern from the divisions
steps.text: Cable LFO out → Hat gate (every eighth), Clock div d2 → kick gate (every beat) and Clock div d4 → snare gate (every second beat). Remove the cable from Main’s gate to the Hat.

parts.label: Cable LFO out → Hat gate
Remove the old cable Main gate → Hat gate (click it)

steps.title: Mix the kit
steps.text: Add a Mixer 4: kick out → in1, snare out → in2, Hat out → in3, and Mixer out → Output l and r. Remove the Hat’s own cable to Output. Set l1 to 0.9 and l3 to 0.4.

parts.label: Cable Hat out → Mixer in3
Cable Mixer out → Output l
Cable Mixer out → Output r
Set Mixer l1 to 0.9
Set Mixer l3 to 0.4
Remove the old cable Hat out → Output l (click it)

steps.title: Place the backbeat
steps.text: Build the beat below: three Sequencers replace the divider gates. At 120 bpm, kick lands on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, and hats on each beat. A step at −1 is a rest; 0 is a hit. Optional: change one rest into an extra hit and listen to the push it creates.
steps.why: Each Sequencer receives the same 4 Hz clock. Its gate triggers one drum. The engine advances on the first tick, so the first sounding slot is s2; s1 is the last eighth of the bar.

steps.title: An eight-bar miniature
steps.text: Build the arrangement below, adding steady eighth-note hats. Bars 1–2 establish your beat; 3–6 add your saved Pluck melody; bar 7 opens the hats for a flourish; bar 8 returns to the beat. It repeats every 16 seconds at 120 bpm. Change the kick Sequencer’s hit values to change the melody; expand Eight-bar arrangement to change the form; your patch stores the performance.
steps.why: One divider ticks once per bar. A slow Sequencer brings in the melody and lengthens the hat tail for a flourish. The same clock drives the notes and the form. If you skipped Pluck, the bundled instrument stands in for it.

steps.title: Share it
steps.text: Commands → Share patch link copies a link to this patch to your clipboard. Anyone who opens it gets the beat, your Pluck instrument and the eight-bar arrangement. Name and save a personal variation at the finish.
